messages.subject: Data with few initial captures
parts:
Hello,
I'm new to SECR and have nobody with any experience at my school to work with. I'm working through the Spatial Capture Recapture book (Royle et al. 2014) to try and figure things out. I believe that I have it partially figured out but experience several issues (although I'm not 100% sure that using multi is appropriate, since I only caught 2 mice in one sherman trap a handful of times). When I was trapping, several of my sites didn't get any captures on the initial trapping session. Meaning I'm able to get my encounter and trapping data files read, but when I try to run a model, I get the following:
Error in secr.fit(capturedata, model = list(D ~ 1, g0 ~ b, sigma ~ 1),  : 
  too few values session 1 to determine start; 
set manually or select different session with details autoini

Can anybody help in explaining how to set manually or select a different session? Does this mean to just start with a session that had more captures?

Also, I really want to figure out how to calculate density. I will include the code and readout below for one trapping grid that worked, and will ask for assistance to see if I am correctly interpreting the output.

I want to end up with Jolly-Seber models to look at survival and density and compare across trapping region. Is this doable? Since I haven't come across JS models in the package vignette, but it does seem like you can do it with spatial aspects using JAGS/BUGS.

Thanks for the assistance.

Lauren

#Here I am just running basic models as described in SECR book#
#This is for small mammal data over 3 field seasons#

setwd("C:/Users/Lauren Paul/Desktop/Final for R/Treated/BGU Directory")
library(secr)
trap=read.csv("bgtraplocs.csv")

trapfile<-read.traps(data=trap,detector="multi")
plot(trapfile)
EDF=read.csv("bg1EDF.csv",header=TRUE)

capturedata<-make.capthist(EDF,trapfile,fmt="trapID",noccasions = 6)
summary(capturedata)
plot(capturedata)

closure.test(capturedata,SB=FALSE)# This means I have an open population

#####################################################################################################
#1)Null model with a bivariate normal encounter probability model
mouse_0=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~1,sigma~1),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################2)Null model with an exponential encounter probability model
mouse_0exp=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~1,sigma~1),detectfn = 2,buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
#3)model with fixed time effects
mouse_t=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~t,sigma~1),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
#4)global behavioral model
mouse_B=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~b,sigma~1),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
#5)trap-specific behavioral response
mouse_b=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~bk,sigma~1),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
#6)global behavioral model with fixed time effects
mouse_bt=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~b+t,sigma~1),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
#7)sex-specific model
mouse_sex=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~session,g0~session,sigma~session),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
#8)heterogeneity model
mouse_h2=secr.fit(capturedata,model=list(D~1,g0~h2,sigma~h2),buffer=300)
#####################################################################################################
model.average(mouse_0,mouse_0exp,mouse_b,mouse_B,mouse_bt,mouse_h2,mouse_sex,mouse_t,realnames = "D")

AIC(mouse_0,mouse_0exp,mouse_b,mouse_B,mouse_bt,mouse_h2,mouse_sex,mouse_t)

mouse_bt

#Readout#
> model.average(mouse_0,mouse_0exp,mouse_b,mouse_B,mouse_bt,mouse_h2,mouse_sex,mouse_t,realnames = "D")

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Data with few initial captures
parts:
Hi Lauren
You're biting off a whole lot here... Some part answers:
1. See http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-multisession.pdf "Failure of autoini". If that fails try the 'start' argument of secr.fit.
2. There is no public software for maximum-likelihood open-population SECR, yet. But see recent posts.
3. My preference is to not get hung up on closure or model selection and averaging. Get to know 1-2 models first.
4. You have a large buffer, presumably because your mice are very mobile? In this case the mice you catch come from a large area and density is lower than you imagine.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Data with few initial captures
parts:
1. secr.fit by default looks at your first session and constructs suitable starting values based on what it finds. If that fails, the details argument 'autoini' allows you to direct it to look at a different session. If that fails, you can specify actual starting values with something like start = list(D=1, g0=0.1, sigma=10). You should not be calling the autoini function.

2. I think you sort of understand what is going on but are expressing it, well, oddly. 'secr' does not estimate turnover per se (it does fit a model, just not that one). However, in 'secr' you can fit a model that treats each session as an independent unit of data; secr does this by maximising the sum of the session log-likelihoods. Yes, open populationSECR models have some appeal. For complete flexibility you will need to go to BUGS/JAGS or Ben Augustine's GitHub R package mentioned in a recent post, but a fairly functional maximum likelihood version will be available soon.

3. Good

4. OK, but I don't think you need to make the buffer uniform across species: better (or at least faster) to match it to the behaviour of each. Or are you throwing a lot of species into one analysis? I don't understand your point about trap days.

EDF=read.csv("bg1EDF.csv",header=TRUE)

plot(capturedata)

closure.test(capturedata,SB=FALSE)# This means I have an open population
